## Overheard at Biscoe Point

<!--
MF's idea: open with a conversation among penguins, as a block quote. Rough draft from
penguin-names.md, to be worked up. Keep it short: three or four exchanges, then pivot to
"they have a point".
-->

> "Hey Bro, have you noticed? All these scientists measured us up the wazoo, published papers, and now our
> data is famous. They use us to teach statistics and data graphics all over the world. But sadly, they don't even know
> our names, even with those tags on our flippers."
>
> "And why didn't they bother to give us the Big Five personality scales? Those orange Adelies are often
> narcissistic extroverts, not very open to experience. I'm a proud, average Joe Gentoo. Let's teach them a thing or two."

They have a point. The [Palmer penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) are
identified only by numbers: their row numbers in a data frame. Even those aren't stable. They
depend on whether the few birds with missing measurements were dropped: Cyrano, whom you'll meet
shortly, is number 294 in `palmerpenguins::penguins` and number 283 in `heplots::peng`. This post
is an attempt to right this injustice to the 344 birds on Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen islands near
Palmer Station who allowed themselves to be measured for science from 2007 to 2009.
I understand your pain.

<!--

Cyrano and Hook Nose (from my book), the BFG, Tinkerbell and Average Joe (from Cara Thompson).
The question of the post: what makes each of them unusual, and do the names fit?
-->

A few of them do have names. Cara Thompson named four: Cyrano, the BFG, Tinkerbell and
Average Joe. I borrowed Cyrano for my book, and added a Hook Nose of my own. So the questions for this
post are: what makes each of these birds unusual, and do their names fit?


## Naming names

```{r data}
#| code-summary: "Data and the named birds"
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

data(peng, package = "heplots")    # palmerpenguins, 333 complete cases

col <- c(Adelie = "#F37A00", Chinstrap = "#6A3D9A", Gentoo = "#33a02c")

# the named birds, by row number in heplots::peng
named <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~name,         ~namer,
  283, "Cyrano",       "Thompson",
  124, "The BFG",      "Thompson",
  304, "Tinkerbell",   "Thompson",
  166, "Average Joe",  "Thompson",
   10, "Socrates?",    "Friendly",
   35, "Falstaff?",    "Friendly"
)

peng <- peng |>
  mutate(id         = row_number(),
         bill_shape = log(bill_length) - log(bill_depth),
         stoutness  = log(body_mass) / 3 - log(flipper_length)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(z_shape = c(scale(bill_shape)),
         z_stout = c(scale(stoutness))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(named, by = "id") |>
  mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(name), NA, paste0(name, " (", id, ")")))
birds <- filter(peng, !is.na(name))
```

I first got to know the Palmer penguins when I found that they made good examples for methods of
multivariate data visualization. I adopted them as a running example in my book,
[_Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R_](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/), where
they turn up in nearly every chapter.

### Three noteworthy birds

In [Chapter 4](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/04-multivariate_plots.html), I went looking
for multivariate outliers. As in the Bob Marley song, I found "three little birds, at my doorstep."
As I hope to say to my Palmer friends, "Don't worry about a thing, 'cause every little thing gonna be all right."

The first tool I usually use to identify possible outliers in multivariate data is a `heplots::cqplot()`,
which shows the squared Mahalanobis distance, $D^2$, of each bird from the
centroid of all four measures (bill length and depth, flipper length, body mass), taking their
variances and correlations into account, plotted against their $\chi^2$ quantiles in a multivariate normal distribution. 
Three birds came out on top: cases 283, 10 and 35. The
chi-square QQ plot showed that only one of them, 283, is a true outlier. The other two are just the
most unusual of an ordinary lot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cqplot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Chi-square QQ plot of the penguins' squared Mahalanobis distances on the four measures, with a 95% confidence envelope. Only case 283 lies outside it."
library(heplots)
vars <- c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "flipper_length", "body_mass")
DSQ <- Mahalanobis(peng[, vars])

cqplot(peng[, vars],
       id.n = 3,
       col = col[peng$species],
       pch = c(19, 17, 15)[peng$species],
       ref.col = "grey",
       what = "Penguin numeric variables",
       cex.lab = 1.25)
```

Plotting bill length against bill depth with those three labeled, two of them looked odd for their
species. Case 283, a [Chinstrap]{.chinstrap}, has a remarkably long bill, so I called him "Cyrano",
after the long-nosed hero of Edmond Rostand's play. Case 10, an [Adelie]{.adelie} with a short, deep
bill, became "Hook Nose". Case 35 looked unremarkable in that view and stayed nameless.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill-noteworthy
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-cap: "Bill length against bill depth, with 95% data ellipses and regression lines for each species. The three birds with the largest $D^2$ are labeled."
three <- order(DSQ, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
peng_plot <- peng |> mutate(note = id %in% three)

ggplot(peng_plot,
       aes(x = bill_length, y = bill_depth,
           colour = species, shape = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = note), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(1.5, 4)) +
  geom_text(data = subset(peng_plot, note),
            aes(label = id), fontface = "bold",
            nudge_y = .4, colour = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.95, alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.15))
```

The names stuck, at least for me. Cyrano reappears throughout the book: dancing around the edges of a
grand tour, at the extreme ends of a biplot, as the most influential case in a multivariate linear
model, and finally getting a weight of zero in a robust fit. "Bye-bye Cyrano---it's been fun---but we
can get along nicely without you." That is the point of a name: a reader can follow Cyrano from chapter
to chapter in a way they can't follow "case 283".

### Where "Cyrano" came from

I thought I had made up the name. It turns out I hadn't. I'd seen it in
[Cara Thompson](https://www.cararthompson.com/)'s poster for useR! 2022,
[*Level Up Your Labels: Tips and Tricks for Annotating Plots*](https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/),
filed it away, and forgotten where it came from. My code for the book still had a comment,
`# From Cara Thompson`, above her lines that picked out the birds (with her name misspelled, which
didn't help).

Her poster image is a wonderful lesson in plot annotation. Its plot, titled *"Perfectly proportional penguins---with a
few exceptions!"*, shows flipper length against bill length, and replaces a legend and a lot of
explanation with a few well-placed text boxes. Four birds get names and a sentence each:

* **The BFG**: "Sitting comfortably within the cluster of Gentoos, this Adelie penguin defies the
  predictions of his species on both flipper length and bill length."
* **Tinkerbell**: "The smallest penguin in the set defies the odds on weight for her species and
  flipper and bill length."
* **Average Joes**: "The Gentoos tend to stick to their trend, with very few outliers. Heavier
  penguins have longer flippers and longer bills."
* **Cyrano**: "With an exceptionally long bill and the shortest flippers bar one among the
  Chinstraps, this little guy is sure to stand out!"

![Cara Thompson's plot from her useR! 2022 poster, [*Level Up Your Labels*](https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/). © Cara Thompson, reused under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](images/thompson-annotated-penguins.png){#fig-thompson}

She picked these birds by eye, from one plot. As we'll see, every one of her descriptions holds up,
except perhaps "little guy": Cyrano is a female.

### Who gets a label?

Thompson's poster had a second effect on me. In her plot, and in mine in the book, the labeled
birds were chosen by hand, and the labels were added by a small piece of `ggplot2` plumbing: compute
something, make a logical variable for the cases to label, then add a `geom_text()` layer for just
those rows. It works, but you have to do it again for every plot.

Base R graphics handle this better than `ggplot2`, thanks to the `car` package. Nearly every plotting
function in `car` takes an argument like `id = list(n = 3, method = "mahal")`, and labels the 3
points furthest from the centroid, with no further work. The `method` can be `"x"`, `"y"`, `"r"` for
residuals, or a vector such as Cook's distances. Labeling unusual points becomes a decision about
*which criterion*, not a chore.

I pulled that selection logic out into a function,
[`heplots::noteworthy()`](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/reference/noteworthy.html), which takes
`x`, `y`, `n` and a `method`, and returns the row numbers of the points to label. The criterion
needn't come from the two variables on the axes. Here it finds the book's three birds, using $D^2$ on
all four measures, for a plot of just two:

```{r noteworthy}
#| code-fold: show
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 3, method = DSQ)
```

That isn't what Thompson would have found with a formula. The default, `method = "mahal"`, on the
two variables in her plot picks out a different set:

```{r noteworthy-2d}
#| code-fold: show
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 6, method = "mahal")
```

Cyrano (283) is first again, but the rest (179, 314, 272, ...) are birds on the edges of the overall
cloud, which spans three species. None of the BFG, Tinkerbell or Average Joe is on that list. Her eye
was doing something the formula wasn't: judging each bird *against its own species*. I'll come back to
that.

The next step was to make this a `ggplot2` layer, `stat_noteworthy()`, so that any plot could say
which points to label in the same vocabulary. With help from the
[ggplot2 extenders club](https://github.com/ggplot2-extenders/ggplot-extension-club/discussions/91),
I got a working version. Getting it *generally* right turned out to be harder:

<!-- MF: check/expand. From heplots/dev/noteworthy/ggextenders-noteworthy.md -->

* **With groups**, should it pick the $n$ most unusual points overall, or $n$ in each group? The
  usual `ggplot2` habit is per group. A statistician usually wants the most unusual points in the
  plot as a whole. Both are reasonable, so it should probably be an option.
* **With facets**, the selection should be done separately in each panel.
* **Higher dimensions**: the penguins' case is the hardest. The criterion ($D^2$ over four variables)
  lives in more dimensions than the plot shows. A `ggplot2` stat sees only the variables mapped to
  aesthetics, so there's no clean way to hand it the others.

So `stat_noteworthy()` is still in the development folder of `heplots`, a branch partly leafed out,
waiting for another season. Meanwhile the penguins wait for their names.

## One view in 2D

To see the six birds together, @fig-thompson-view reproduces Thompson's plot, without her
annotations: flipper length against bill length, with the size of each point showing body mass.
Her four named birds and my two are labeled with their case numbers in `heplots::peng`.

Her four are easy to find. Cyrano is alone at the right, far beyond the other Chinstraps. The BFG is an
orange point among the green Gentoos. Tinkerbell is the smallest point among the Chinstraps, and Average
Joe sits in the middle of the Gentoos. But Socrates and Falstaff don't stand out. Socrates is at the
short-bill edge of the Adelies, but not beyond it, and Falstaff is lost in the crowd. What makes them
unusual will need another view.

```{r}
#| label: fig-thompson-view
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Thompson's view of the penguins: flipper length against bill length, with point size showing body mass. Her four named birds are joined by two more from my book."
ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length, flipper_length, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = body_mass), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = birds, aes(size = body_mass), shape = 21,
             colour = "black", stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_size(range = c(0.5, 7), breaks = c(3000, 4500, 6000),
             labels = \(x) paste(x / 1000, "kg")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species", size = "Body mass") +
  guides(size = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "grey50")),
         colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.02, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1), legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))
```

## What makes a penguin unusual?

To say *why* a bird is unusual, you need a better question than "which of its four measures is
extreme?" A long bill is only part of a description: is it also deep, or unusually slender? And a
heavy penguin may just be a big penguin. The two earlier posts in this series took up exactly
these questions, by re-expressing the four measures as variables that mean something:

* In [Thinking about Penguin Variables](https://friendly.github.io/blog/posts/2026-10-peng-altviews/),
  bill length ($L$) and depth ($D$) became bill **size**, $\log L + \log D$, and bill **shape**,
  $\log (L / D)$: is the bill long and slender, or short and stubby?
* In [Penguin Bodies](https://friendly.github.io/blog/posts/2026-10-peng-body/), flipper length
  ($F$) and body mass ($M$) became body **size**, $\log F + \log M / 3$, and **stoutness**,
  $\log (M^{1/3} / F)$: is the bird heavy or light for its flipper length? Cubed, this is
  $M / F^3$, a penguin version of the condition factor used for fish.

Within species, these four are nearly uncorrelated, except that bigger birds have bigger bills
(bill size with body size, $r = 0.70$). The two size variables mostly say what you'd expect: big
birds are big all over. What gives a bird its character is its *proportions*, and those are what the
names are about: a long nose, a snub nose, a stout body, a slight one. So here I use just the two
ratios, bill shape and stoutness. Both are dimensionless, and they are almost exactly uncorrelated
within species ($r = -0.03$).

The second question is: unusual *compared with whom?* Cyrano's bill, at 3.26 times as long as it is
deep, would be unremarkable on a [Gentoo]{.gentoo}, whose bills average 3.18. On a
[Chinstrap]{.chinstrap}, it is the most slender bill by a wide margin. A Gentoo's bill on a Gentoo
isn't news; on a Chinstrap it is. So I standardize each variable *within species*: a bird's
$z$-score is its distance from its own species' mean, in units of that species' standard deviation.
This also puts the species on a common scale, which matters because they don't vary equally:
[Adelie]{.adelie} bills vary more in shape than the others. Males and females are pooled. Males are
bigger, but on these two ratios the sexes differ little, except that Adelie males are a bit stouter.

This is where Thompson's eye and the book's formula parted company. The book's $D^2$ measured each
bird's distance from the centroid of *all* the penguins, ignoring species. By that measure the BFG
ranks 89th of 333: a large Adelie sits comfortably inside the overall cloud, close to the
Gentoos. Judged against other Adelies, with the same $D^2$ computed within species, he is the third
most unusual bird in the data. Thompson saw that from one plot.

@tbl-birds gives the six birds' bill ratios and stoutness indices as recorded, and their $z$-scores
within species. The raw measurements are in the [next section](#do-the-names-fit) below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-birds
#| tbl-cap: "The named birds: bill length / depth and the stoutness index M / F³ (in g/cm³), as recorded, and bill shape and stoutness as z-scores within species. Species means of L / D are 2.12 (Adelie), 2.65 (Chinstrap) and 3.18 (Gentoo); of M / F³, 0.54, 0.50 and 0.50."
birds |>
  mutate(name   = factor(name, levels = named$name[c(1, 5, 6, 3, 2, 4)]),
         LD     = bill_length / bill_depth,
         MF3    = 1000 * body_mass / flipper_length^3) |>
  arrange(name) |>
  select(name, id, species, sex, LD, MF3, z_shape, z_stout) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Name", "Case", "Species", "Sex", "L / D", "M / F³",
                             "z shape", "z stoutness"))
```

@fig-shape-stoutness is the main event: every bird, placed by bill shape and stoutness within its
species. Because the two are nearly uncorrelated and on the same scale, it reads like a map. An
ordinary penguin sits near the center; the farther a bird lies from it, in any direction, the more
unusual it is; and the *direction* says why. To the right, slender bills; to the left, stubby ones.
Up is stout, down is lean.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-stoutness
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-cap: "Bill shape against stoutness, as z-scores within species. The ellipses enclose about 68% and 95% of the birds. The named birds lie in contrasting directions from the center; Average Joe marks the center itself."
lim <- c(-4.2, 4.2)
ggplot(peng, aes(z_shape, z_stout, colour = species)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.95, colour = "grey40",
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.68, colour = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = birds, shape = 21, size = 3.5, colour = "black",
             aes(fill = species), stroke = 1.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.7, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  coord_equal(xlim = lim, ylim = lim) +
  labs(x = "← stubby    Bill shape, z within species    slender →",
       y = "← lean    Stoutness, z within species    stout →",
       colour = "Species") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.88, 0.14),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))
```

The named birds spread out to the edges, in pairs of opposites. Cyrano lies far to the right, the
most slender bill for her species, and Socrates far to the left, among the stubbiest: the long nose
and the snub nose. Falstaff is at the top and Tinkerbell at the bottom: the stoutest and the
slightest. The BFG is off in the lower right, with a slender bill and a lean body, not the most
extreme on either alone, but unusual on both. Average Joe sits almost exactly at the center.

Two of these birds were hard to see in Thompson's view (@fig-thompson-view). Socrates' bill is
short, but no shorter than a few other Adelies', and Falstaff's flippers are short, but not
remarkably so. What marks them out is a ratio: bill
length to depth for Socrates, mass to flipper length for Falstaff. A plot of the raw measures can't
show a ratio unless you know to look for it.

The map also turns up birds that nobody has named yet. The stubbiest bill for its species isn't
Socrates' but that of a Gentoo male, case 183 (z = −3.93, against −3.43 for Socrates). Socrates has
the stubbiest bill of all 333 as measured, at 1.64, but Adelie bills are stubby to begin with.
Likewise, two Gentoo males, 160 and 253, are as stout among Gentoos as Falstaff is among Adelies.

## Do the names fit?

A name is a one-word theory of what makes a bird unusual. Here are the six, in the pairs of the
map, with their measurements and a verdict on each name. Comparisons in parentheses are with the
mean for the bird's species and sex.

### Cyrano (283): the long nose

Cyrano, a [Chinstrap]{.chinstrap} female, has the longest bill of any Chinstrap: 58.0 mm (46.6).
But its depth is ordinary, 17.8 mm (17.6), so it is long *and* slender. At 3.26 times as long as it is
deep, it is far beyond any other Chinstrap's (the next is 2.93), and more slender than the average
[Gentoo]{.gentoo} bill. She has a Gentoo's bill on a Chinstrap's body. She is also stout, the
second part of her story: a normal mass, 3700 g (3527), on flippers of 181 mm (192), among the
shortest of the Chinstraps. Thompson's label, "an exceptionally long bill and the shortest flippers
bar one among the Chinstraps", is exact.

**Verdict:** The name fits perfectly. Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac has the most famous nose in
literature, the subject of a whole speech in the play: "C'est un roc! … c'est un pic! … c'est un cap!
Que dis-je, c'est un cap? … C'est une péninsule!" (It's a rock, a peak, a cape! A cape, did I say?
It's a peninsula!) That Cyrano is a female, which Thompson's "little guy" missed,
doesn't matter. A nose like that transcends gender.

### Socrates (10): the snub nose, formerly Hook Nose

Case 10, an [Adelie]{.adelie} male, has the opposite bill: short, 34.6 mm (40.4), and deep,
21.1 mm (19.1), at the 4th and 97th percentiles of the Adelies. Its ratio of 1.64 (2.12) is the
lowest of all 333 penguins; the next is 1.76. The rest of him is a large but ordinary Adelie male.

I called him "Hook Nose" in the book, describing "a very short and curved bill." That was my mistake:
bill depth is measured top to bottom at the base of the bill. It says how *thick* the bill is, not how
curved. Nothing in the data measures a hook. What he has is a snub nose.

**Verdict:** "Hook Nose" doesn't fit; **Socrates** does. His snub nose is the best documented in
history. Plato and Xenophon both mention it, and in Xenophon's *Symposium* Socrates argues, tongue in
cheek, that it is the more beautiful kind, because upturned nostrils catch scents from every
direction. Cyrano and Socrates make a pair, the long nose and the snub nose: one has a bill too
slender for her species, the other too stubby for his. One caveat, from the map: relative to its own
species, the stubbiest bill belongs to Gentoo 183, still nameless.

### Falstaff (35): the stout one

Case 35, another Adelie male, has a bill that is average in every respect: 39.8 by 19.1 mm, against
means of 40.4 and 19.1. It is his body that stands out. At 4650 g (4043), he is one of the
heaviest Adelies, 97th percentile, but his flippers are short, 184 mm (192). That makes him, on the
raw index M/F³ = 0.75, the stoutest penguin in the data; the next is 0.69. (Within species, two
Gentoos are as extreme, relative to other Gentoos.) In the book (Chapter 5), he showed up at
the edge of a biplot of the smallest principal components, where I guessed that he was "probably much
heavier than most and has short flippers". That was right, but I didn't give him a name.

**Verdict:** **Falstaff**, Shakespeare's fat knight in *Henry IV*, who pleads "banish plump Jack, and
banish all the world." He is a new name, so the only question is whether it fits. I think it does.

### Tinkerbell (304): the slight one

Tinkerbell, a Chinstrap female, is the lightest penguin in the data: 2700 g (3527); the next
lightest weighs 2850 g. But she is not simply small. Her flippers, 192 mm, are exactly the average
for a Chinstrap female, and her bill is an ordinary length, if shallow. She is light *for her size*.
On M/F³ = 0.38, she is the least stout bird of all 333, and the most extreme on stoutness within
species too. She is Falstaff's mirror image: his M/F³ is 31% above the mean for Adelie males, hers 24% below
the mean for Chinstrap females.

**Verdict:** Thompson's label calls her "the smallest penguin in the set." "Lightest" is more precise,
since her flippers are ordinary. But Barrie's Tinker Bell is a tiny fairy, and the name suits a bird
that weighs less than she should. It fits. (Barrie did describe his Tinker Bell as "slightly inclined
to *embonpoint*", but we needn't tell her.)

### The BFG (124): the impostor

The BFG is an Adelie male with the longest flippers of any Adelie: 210 mm (192); the next is 208. His
bill is long for an Adelie, 44.1 mm (40.4), but shallower, 18.0 mm (19.1), so it is slender. He is
not heavy: 4000 g (4043). Long flippers on an ordinary mass make him lean.

In Thompson's view, flipper length against bill length, he sits "comfortably within the cluster of
Gentoos". A discriminant analysis on just those two variables would call him a Gentoo, with a
posterior probability of 0.97. On all four measures, it wouldn't. His bill is still deep for a Gentoo.
None of his oddities is extreme on its own, which is why the book's $D^2$, ignoring species, ranked
him 89th. Taken together, against other Adelies, he is the third most unusual bird in the data.

**Verdict:** It fits beautifully. Dahl's Big Friendly Giant is the gentle runt among giants, much
smaller than the others. That's the BFG here: a giant among Adelies, but a small Gentoo.

### Average Joe (166): the reference bird

Thompson's text box was for the "Average Joes", plural: the [Gentoo]{.gentoo}s, who "tend to stick
to their trend, with very few outliers." The bird her arrow points to is Gentoo male 166, and he is
average indeed. His flippers, 222 mm, are exactly the mean for a Gentoo male. His bill, 48.7 by
15.1 mm (49.5 by 15.7), and his mass, 5350 g (5485), are close to it. On the map, he sits near the
center (z = 0.31 and −0.17). Among all 333 birds, by $D^2$ within species, he ranks 319th: only 14
birds are more ordinary.

**Verdict:** It fits, and it earns its place. Every gallery of oddities needs one ordinary specimen
to show what "normal" looks like. He is the reference bird.

## What's in a name?

Thompson's names come from fiction: Rostand's Cyrano, Barrie's Tinker Bell, Dahl's Big Friendly
Giant, and the everyman. Each one describes a body, not a personality. Socrates and Falstaff are meant
to join that family: one from history by way of Plato, one from Shakespeare. Together they make three
pairs. Cyrano and Socrates are the long nose and the snub nose; Falstaff and Tinkerbell, the stoutest
and the slightest; the BFG, an Adelie who passes for a Gentoo, and Average Joe, a Gentoo who passes
for nothing but himself.

There is a statistical point under the fun. **A name helps us remember a point; a good choice of
variables tells us *why* it is unusual.** The book's $D^2$, computed on the four measures as recorded
and ignoring species, found Cyrano, Socrates and Falstaff, but ranked the BFG 89th. Thompson's plot of two
raw measures found Cyrano, the BFG and Tinkerbell, but Socrates and Falstaff looked ordinary there.
I misread my own plot and named a bird for a hook that nothing in the data could measure. Once the
measures were re-expressed as bill shape and stoutness, and each bird was compared with its own
species, every one of the six landed in a place that said what was special about it, and the names
could be checked against that. Of the five names these birds had before, four hold up; Hook Nose
has been retired with thanks.

That leaves birds that are just as unusual and still go by a row number. Gentoo male 183 has the
stubbiest bill for his species, stubbier relative to other Gentoos than Socrates' is among the Adelies.
"Pug" would do, or "Puffin", if naming a penguin after another bird isn't an insult. Gentoo males 160
and 253 are as stout as Falstaff, relative to their species. Suggestions are welcome: in the
comments, or wherever you found this post.

As for the penguins of Biscoe Point, a few of them can now be called by their names. The Big Five
personality scales will have to wait for another field season.

[]{#about-the-banner}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## About the banner

The banner image was made by ChatGPT, not drawn from the data. I asked it to read an earlier draft of
this post, with @tbl-birds, and to design a banner of the six birds: in sunglasses, in my species
colors, and with sizes, shapes and bills that reflect their measurements. It took four rounds: tinting the bellies
so the species could be told apart at thumbnail size, making Cyrano's bill longer, and adding the
sashes with their names.

It's a caricature, and an instructive one. Cyrano's bill was doubled on purpose, to make the point
at banner size. But Average Joe is too big. The prompt described him, correctly, as having
"the largest overall frame" of the six, as a Gentoo male should. In the picture he stands about half
again as tall as Tinkerbell. In the data, he is only about 20% bigger in each linear dimension than
she is (taking body size, $F \times M^{1/3}$, as the measure), and about 12% bigger than Falstaff.
The image generator read "largest" as "much the largest". Which makes, in its way, the point of
the post: Average Joe is average *for a Gentoo*, and how unusual a bird looks depends on what you
compare it with.
:::

## Further reading

**The earlier posts in this series**

* [Thinking about Penguin Variables](https://friendly.github.io/blog/posts/2026-10-peng-altviews/):
  bill size and shape as an alternative view of bill length and depth.
* [Penguin Bodies: Size and Stoutness](https://friendly.github.io/blog/posts/2026-10-peng-body/):
  the same idea for flipper length and body mass.

**Naming and labeling points**

* Thompson, C. (2022). *Level Up Your Labels: Tips and Tricks for Annotating Plots*. Poster, useR! 2022.
  <https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/>
* Friendly, M. (in preparation). *Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R*. Chapman & Hall/CRC.
  Online at <https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/>. Cyrano and his companions first appear in
  [Chapter 4](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/04-multivariate_plots.html), and come back in
  the chapter on influence and robust estimation for multivariate models.
* Friendly, M., Fox, J., & Monette, G. *heplots: Visualizing Tests in Multivariate Linear Models*.
  R package. <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=heplots>. See
  [`noteworthy()`](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/reference/noteworthy.html).
* Fox, J., & Weisberg, S. (2018). *An R Companion to Applied Regression* (3rd ed.). Sage. The `car`
  package, whose `id` argument labels unusual points in nearly every plot.

**The data**

* Gorman, K. B., Williams, T. D., & Fraser, W. R. (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and
  environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus *Pygoscelis*).
  *PLoS ONE*, 9(3), e90081. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0090081>
* Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). *palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica)
  penguin data*. R package version 0.1.0. <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218>

**The namesakes**

* Edmond Rostand, [*Cyrano de Bergerac*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrano_de_Bergerac_(play)) (1897).
  The nose speech is in Act I, scene 4.
* Xenophon, [*Symposium*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symposium_(Xenophon)), chapter 5: Socrates'
  beauty contest with Critobulus, nose included.
* William Shakespeare, [*Henry IV, Part 1*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV,_Part_1) (c. 1597),
  for [Falstaff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falstaff).
* J. M. Barrie, [*Peter and Wendy*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_and_Wendy) (1911), for
  [Tinker Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinker_Bell).
* Roald Dahl, [*The BFG*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_BFG) (1982).
